title: The Monkey’s Paw
author: W. W. Jacobs
summary: Numa noite fria e chuvosa, a família White recebe a visita de um velho soldado que voltou da Índia. Ele traz uma pata de macaco seca e diz que ela tem um poder mágico: pode realizar três desejos. Mas ele avisa que a pata é perigosa e que o destino não gosta de ser desafiado. É um conto de terror clássico sobre desejos, sorte e medo.

chapters.title: A Visitor on a Cold Night
paragraphs: It is a cold, wet night. The wind is loud outside the little house. Inside, the fire is bright. Mr. White and his son, Herbert, are playing chess. Mrs. White is knitting by the fire.
“Listen to the wind,” says Mr. White.
“I'm listening,” says Herbert. He moves a piece. “Check.”
“This place is terrible,” says his father. “The road is all mud. Nobody comes here.”
Then they hear the gate. Mr. White jumps up. “That's him! That's Morris!”
He opens the door. A tall, strong man comes in. His face is red from the sun. His name is Sergeant-Major Morris. He is an old friend of Mr. White. For twenty-one years he was a soldier in India.
They sit by the fire. Mr. White gives him a glass of whisky. Morris tells them stories of wild places, of wars and of strange people. The family listens with big eyes.
“I want to go to India,” says Mr. White.
“Better where you are,” says the soldier. He shakes his head.
“Tell us about the monkey's paw, Morris,” says Mr. White. “You talked about it once.”
“Oh, it's nothing,” says Morris quickly. “Only a bit of magic, maybe.”
The family looks at him. They are very curious now.

chapters.title: Three Wishes
paragraphs: Morris takes something from his pocket. It is small, brown and dry. It looks like a little dead hand.
“This is the monkey's paw,” he says.
Mrs. White pulls back. “Ugh!” she says. But Herbert takes it and looks at it.
“What is special about it?” asks Mr. White.
“An old holy man in India put a spell on it,” says Morris. “He wanted to show something. Fate rules our lives. People who fight fate are sorry. With this paw, three men can have three wishes each.”
“And you?” asks Herbert. “Did you have your three wishes?”
“I did,” says Morris quietly. His face goes white.
“And the first man? Did he have his wishes?”
“Yes. I don't know his first two wishes. But his third wish was for death. That's how I got the paw.”
The room is very quiet.
Then Morris suddenly throws the paw into the fire. Mr. White gives a cry and pulls it out.
“Burn it,” says Morris. “It's better.”
“But I want it,” says Mr. White. “How do I use it?”
“Hold it up in your right hand and say your wish out loud. But I am warning you. Bad things can happen.”
“It sounds like a story from the Arabian Nights,” says Mrs. White. She laughs. “Wish for four pairs of hands for me!”
Morris does not laugh. “If you must wish,” he says, “wish for something sensible.”
Later, Morris leaves. Herbert laughs at his father. “Wish to be an emperor, Father! Then Mother can't tell you what to do!”
“I have everything I want,” says Mr. White. “But we need two hundred pounds to finish paying for the house.”
He holds up the paw. “I wish for two hundred pounds,” he says.
Then he cries out and drops it. “It moved! It moved in my hand like a snake!”
There is no money. They laugh and go to bed. But the room feels cold.

chapters.title: The Man from Maw and Meggins
paragraphs: The next morning, the sun is shining. The paw is on the table. It looks small and silly now. Everybody laughs about it at breakfast.
“Maybe the money falls on your head from the sky, Father,” says Herbert. Then he goes to work at the factory. “Don't spend it before I come back!” he shouts at the door.
In the afternoon, Mrs. White sees a man outside the gate. He is wearing good clothes. He walks to the gate, then away, then back again. At last he comes in.
“I come from Maw and Meggins,” he says. He looks nervous. “That's the factory.”
Mrs. White's heart stops. “Is it Herbert? What's wrong? Is he hurt?”
“He is badly hurt,” says the man. “But he is not in any pain now.”
“Oh, thank God!” says Mrs. White. Then she understands. Her face goes white. “Not in any pain…”
The man looks at the floor. “He was caught in the machinery,” he says quietly.
Mr. White takes his wife's hand. For a long time nobody speaks.
“The company is very sorry,” says the man. “They don't accept any responsibility. But because of your son's work, they want to give you some money.”
Mr. White stands up. “How much?” he whispers.
“Two hundred pounds.”
Mrs. White screams. Mr. White falls to the floor.

chapters.title: The Second Wish
paragraphs: They bury Herbert in a big new cemetery, two miles away. Then they come back to a dark and silent house. Days pass. The old couple hardly speak.
About a week later, Mr. White wakes up in the night. His wife is not in bed. She is crying by the window.
“Come back to bed,” he says. “It's cold.”
“It's colder for my son,” she says.
Then suddenly she cries out. “The paw! The monkey's paw!”
“What? Where is it? What's the matter?”
“I want it! We have two more wishes. Wish for our boy to come back!”
“You are mad!” says Mr. White. He is afraid.
“Go and get it. Go now!”
He goes down in the dark. The paw is in its place. He brings it to her.
“Wish!” she says.
“It's foolish and wicked,” he says. “You didn't see him. His face was terrible. I knew him only from his clothes.”
“Wish!” she cries. “Do you think I'm afraid of my own child?”
He holds up the paw. “I wish my son alive again.”
The paw falls to the floor. He shakes. His wife goes to the window and waits.
Nothing happens. The candle burns down and goes out. The old man goes back to bed. After a minute, his wife comes too. She is silent.

chapters.title: Knocking at the Door
paragraphs: They lie in the dark. They do not sleep. The clock ticks. A stair creaks. A mouse runs in the wall.
Mr. White cannot stand it. He gets up to find a match. He goes down the stairs in the dark.
Then he hears it. There is a knock at the front door. It is very quiet. He stands still and does not breathe. There is another knock. He runs back up to the bedroom and closes the door.
A third knock sounds through the house.
“What's that?” cries his wife. She sits up.
“A rat,” he says. “It's only a rat.”
“It's Herbert!” she screams. “It's Herbert! I forgot the cemetery is two miles away. That's why he is so late! I must open the door!”
“For God's sake, don't let it in!” cries the old man. He holds her arm.
“You are afraid of your own son!” she cries. She pulls her arm free. “I'm coming, Herbert! I'm coming!”
She runs down the stairs. He hears her at the door. The knocking is louder now. It does not stop. She pulls at the chain. “The bolt!” she cries. “I can't reach the top bolt. Come down and help me!”
But the old man is on his hands and knees. He is looking for the paw on the floor. He must find it before the thing outside comes in.
The knocks are very loud now. They shake the whole house. He hears his wife pull a chair to the door. He hears the bolt move.
At that moment, his hand finds the monkey's paw. He holds it up and says his third and last wish.
The knocking stops at once. The house is silent. He hears the chair go back. He hears the door open. A cold wind comes up the stairs.
His wife gives a long, sad cry. He runs down to her, and then out to the gate. The street lamp is shining on a quiet, empty road.
